title: Box Tree Moth Caterpillar Damage: How to Spot It and What to Do
metaDescription: How to identify box tree moth caterpillar damage on a box hedge, why it matters in Kent gardens, and what the RHS actually recommends for control.
ogDescription: How to spot it early and what the RHS recommends, before it strips a box hedge bare.
h1: Box tree moth caterpillar damage: how to spot it and what to do
lede: Box tree moth has gone from a rare sighting to established in every English county since it first turned up in UK gardens in 2008. If you've got box hedging in Kent, it's worth knowing what to look for.

sections.h2: What the damage actually looks like
paras: The caterpillars eat box leaves and spin webbing over the area they're feeding on, so the first sign is often patchy, papery-looking foliage with fine webbing rather than obvious holes. Newly hatched caterpillars are greenish-yellow with black heads. Mature caterpillars grow to around 4cm, with a greenish-yellow body marked with thick black and thin white stripes, easy to spot once you know what you're looking for.
Left unchecked, caterpillars can also strip bark from stems, which can girdle and kill whole sections of the plant, not just the leaves.

The RHS recommends regular inspection from early spring, with checks stepping up from May onward as moth activity increases. Catching an infestation early, before it's stripped a section of hedge bare, makes a real difference to how much of the plant survives.

Where it's practical, the RHS's first suggestion is simply removing caterpillars by hand. For monitoring adult moth activity, pheromone traps (RHS names Agralan, Dragonfli and Solabiol as suppliers) help track when moths are active so you know when to check more closely.

For treatment, a nematode-based product is the RHS's recommended biological control, though they flag it needs some caution around effects on non-target insects. Some trade sources also point to Bacillus thuringiensis (Btk) sprays, which aren't the RHS's own headline recommendation but are widely used and reportedly effective when caterpillars are actively feeding, worth checking product labelling rather than assuming any one product is a like-for-like swap.

If an infestation keeps coming back year after year or a hedge is already heavily defoliated, the RHS's own fallback is honest: consider a different hedge or topiary species if control stops being practical.

sections.h2: What this means for a Kent garden
paras: Box hedging and topiary are common in Sandwich, Deal and the surrounding villages, especially in older, formal gardens, so this isn't a rare problem here. A spring check before growth really gets going, and another through May and June, catches most infestations before they do serious damage.

extractionNotes: Facts checked directly against the RHS's own box tree caterpillar page (rhs.org.uk/biodiversity/box-tree-caterpillar) before writing. RHS's own headline biological control recommendation is a nematode product, not Btk, per the page's actual wording, deliberately not merged with secondary trade-source claims about Btk sprays which are attributed separately and not presented as RHS's own recommendation. No invented product names or efficacy figures.
